findings.claim: The at-most-one-page-group-per-tensor bound, and the background-thread overlap built on it, assume decode produces exactly one token per iteration. Steps that add several tokens could cross page boundaries and need more mappings than the overlap prepared. The paper does not discuss this case.
conditions: The serving framework runs multi-token steps in decode-like iterations
The added tokens cross a page-group boundary
findings.mechanism: General knowledge: speculative decoding verifies several draft tokens per iteration, and chunked prefill processes a block of prompt tokens per iteration. Either can add more tokens than fit in the already mapped page-group. The step API itself takes arbitrary sequence lengths and computes prefill demand as (s+t-1)/t, so it can map more pages. But the decode latency-hiding in §6.1.1 relies on knowing demand one iteration ahead from a single-token increment. A larger step could make the next iteration's mappings fall back to the synchronous path, which costs about 5 ms per request for Yi-34B.

findings.claim: Deferred reclamation defers the unmap and release work rather than removing it. The paper triggers reclamation only below a threshold and delegates it to a background thread. Near serving capacity, idle pages held in finished slots reduce free memory for admission, so reclamation is more likely to run during load. The paper gives no evidence on whether that work stays hidden.
conditions: Cached idle page-groups approach the reclamation threshold under load
The background thread is slower than the demand for freed memory
A step must wait for reclaimed memory before it can proceed
findings.mechanism: Memory held in cached slots is unavailable for other allocations until reclaimed. Unmap plus release at 2MB costs about 34µs + 23µs per call (Table 3). A step that needs memory must wait if the background thread has not freed it yet. Under memory pressure the reclamation cost returns, and it is multiplied across 2N tensors. If the background thread lags, the cost can surface as a latency spike in the step that needs the memory. The paper evaluates a single 16K prefill and does not test this regime.

findings.claim: Keeping the KV cache virtually contiguous with on-demand physical mapping only reduces fragmentation if the physical page-group is small. Waste per request therefore scales with page size times the number of independently backed tensors (2N), not with the number of requests alone. The 'no fragmentation' property comes from decoupling plus small page-groups, not from decoupling alone. Without the modified driver (64KB to 256KB), stock CUDA 2MB pages leave much of the fragmentation problem in place, and the paper itself reports lower max batch size with 2MB pages than with 64KB pages.

findings.mechanism: A request's slot index is fixed by reqId, while its position in the current Q batch changes as continuous batching adds and removes requests. A kernel can read the right slot only if it accepts an explicit batch-index mapping or strided addressing. Contiguity avoids Block-Tables, but the slot layout shifts a compatibility requirement from a paging-aware kernel to a batch-index-aware kernel. Kernels without such an argument would need a copy, a repack, or a code change. This is supported by the paper's own note that FlashInfer lacked stride support.

findings.claim: Giving kernels ordinary contiguous per-layer tensors does not by itself make every kernel usable. The kernel must also accept a KV batch dimension that is decoupled from Q (cache_batch_idx-style indexing), and, for the optional tensor-slicing variant, strided addressing.

findings.mechanism: Virtual tensors are indexed by a fixed reqId slot, so finished requests leave unused holes in the batch dimension of the KV tensor. Q is packed only for active requests, so kernels must map Q rows to arbitrary KV slots. The transparency claim depends on kernel API features beyond tensor contiguity. A kernel that assumes Q and KV share one dense batch index would need modification or a copy. The 'no kernel rewrite' benefit is therefore conditional on that API support.

conditions: Pool sizes are fixed or reclaimed only at thresholds.

findings.mechanism: Physical pages taken through the CUDA VMM path and memory taken by PyTorch's cudaMalloc-based caching allocator are separate pools. Neither automatically lends memory to the other. The activation allocator can fail while the KV page pool still has unmapped or cached pages. Activation memory grows with the tokens processed per iteration (for example, large prefill chunks). The paper reports prefill up to 192K, so these configurations evidently fit.

findings.mechanism: A kernel that assumes Q and KV share a packed, identically ordered batch dimension cannot address a KV slot at an arbitrary position. It would need either an equivalent indirection argument or a compacted KV layout. The paper states the hole problem and says FlashAttention's cache_batch_idx solves it. The paper's general portability claim therefore depends on a kernel exposing a comparable argument. This dependence is inferred; the paper does not list which other kernels have such an argument.

findings.claim: A hole left by an exited request stays backed by physical pages under deferred reclamation. The slot design avoids the hole's kernel-layout cost but ties physical memory to idle or reassigned slots until a reclamation threshold is crossed.
conditions: Requests have highly variable context lengths.
Reclamation is triggered only below a cache threshold.
Memory pressure is high enough that retained pages matter.

findings.mechanism: Physical GPU memory that stays mapped to an inactive slot is unavailable to other slots or to other consumers such as activations. The paper says only that virtual space is cheap, not that retained physical pages are free. Between exit and reclamation, an idle reqId holds physical page-groups sized to the previous request's context length, and a later short request that inherits the slot also inherits those pages. This residual retention is inferred from the deferred-reclamation description; the paper does not measure it.

findings.claim: The step API only reports failure when physical pages cannot be mapped. Whether the system then makes progress depends on a preemption policy that the serving framework must supply. The paper describes only a recompute-style default and does not evaluate its cost.
conditions: Memory demand exceeds available physical pages at some iteration
The serving framework's preemption policy is naive, absent, or frees too few pages
findings.mechanism: General knowledge: a status code of -1 only reports that mapping failed. Progress requires some component to free pages by evicting or recomputing requests, and that choice affects latency, wasted work and fairness. Recompute-style preemption discards KV state that must be rebuilt through prefill. The paper says a framework 'can' preempt, so progress is conditional on that policy existing and choosing victims whose freed pages cover the shortfall. The artifact guarantees contiguity and on-demand mapping. It does not guarantee liveness or bounded cost under memory pressure.

findings.claim: The overlap works only while the next iteration's mapping work finishes inside the current iteration. The paper justifies this with a typical iteration latency of 10s-100s of ms. That is a property of the evaluated A100 setups, not of the mechanism.
conditions: Iteration time is short relative to aggregate map-call time

findings.mechanism: Faster GPUs, smaller models, and higher tensor-parallel degree shorten decode iterations. Per-call driver latency is a CPU and driver cost that does not shrink with GPU speed. If iteration time falls while per-iteration map work stays the same or rises, the margin shrinks. The paper reports H100 throughput in Figure 11 but runs the hiding ablation (Figure 12) only on A100.

findings.claim: Reusing a finished request's reqId removes prefill-time mapping only when a finished slot is available and already holds enough page-groups. A burst of arrivals, or a new prompt longer than the old slot's context, still requires mapping on the prefill path. Eager allocation is prepared for only one reqId at a time.
conditions: Arrival rate is not far above exit rate over short windows
Freed slots hold at least as many page-groups as the next prompt needs
The background thread finishes eager mapping before the next arrival
findings.mechanism: A reused slot's mapped size equals what its previous occupant reached. A new prompt larger than that needs the difference mapped. A slot can be reused only after some earlier request has exited. The benefit is bounded by how often a slot is available and by the gap between old and new context lengths. Under a burst of simultaneous arrivals, or when prompts are longer than the freed slots, the remaining mapping falls back on the one eagerly prepared reqId or on synchronous mapping.

findings.claim: The paper's 'no TLB thrashing' result for small page-groups rests on the regular access pattern of the tested attention kernels. It is not a general property of 64KB pages, and it was measured on A100 only.
conditions: The attention kernel streams through the KV cache regularly.
TLB and page-table geometry resembles the A100's.
Kernel runtime in isolation is the relevant metric.
findings.mechanism: TLB reach is entries times page size, so 64KB pages cover 32x less address space per entry than 2MB pages. Whether that matters depends on how much address space a kernel touches within a short window. TLB and page-table geometry differ across GPU generations. By the authors' own attribution, the harmlessness of small pages is conditional on regular, streaming access. A kernel with scattered access, such as sparse or paged-like attention, could exceed TLB reach and lose performance. The A100 result may not carry over to GPUs with different TLB geometry. This consequence is inferred and was not tested in the paper.
